1.text: *In the Name of Allah—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful.* The translation opens with a preposition. There is no verb here, and no subject either. Nothing is actually said to be done in that Name — the sentence simply begins inside it. That incompleteness is deliberate, and it is the first thing to notice. A finished statement would need an object: *I begin reading in the Name of Allah*, or *I begin eating in the Name of Allah*. By leaving the act unspoken, the phrase covers every act. It is not attached to one thing a person does; it is attached to all of them. The historical reason for the instruction is recorded in Maʿārif-ul-Qurʾān. In the Age of Ignorance, before Islam, people began every undertaking with the names of their idols. The very first revelation addressed to the Prophet ﷺ answered that practice head on — *Read in the name of your Lord* (96:1) — and from that point the Name was placed at the front of everything a Muslim sets out to do. **Why a Name, and why these two.** The Arabic *ism* is that by which a thing is known. Al-Jalālayn puts it in one line: the name of a thing is that by which it can be known. So to begin in the Name of Allah is to begin from the point at which He can actually be recognised — not from His essence, which nothing can contain, but from what He has disclosed of Himself. Then come two descriptors, both built on the same root, *r-ḥ-m*, mercy. Al-Mukhtaṣar draws the point out: *ar-Raḥmān* and *ar-Raḥīm* both derive from *raḥmah*, and their pairing is meant to establish the vastness of His mercy — that it surrounds everything and embraces every living being, and that every blessing any creature holds is an outflow of it. The two words are not a repetition. Maʿārif notes that both are intensive forms in Arabic, and that they connote respectively the superabundance and the perfection of divine mercy. Al-Jalālayn separates them further: *ar-Raḥmān* is the One who causes existence and perfection to flow upon all things, in the measure that divine wisdom requires; *ar-Raḥīm* is the One who bestows the spiritual perfection reserved for human beings in the Hereafter. Hence the classical formulation — you may say *O Compassionate One of this world and of the Hereafter*, but you say *O Merciful One of the Hereafter*. **Is this verse part of the sūrah?** The jurists disagreed about it, and the disagreement is worth knowing because it explains something visible in any printed copy of the Qurʾān. There is consensus, Maʿārif records, that *Bismillāh* is a verse of the Qurʾān — it stands unambiguously inside Sūrah an-Naml, at 27:30. There is agreement too that it is written at the head of every sūrah except at-Tawbah. What the mujtahids differed on is whether it forms an integral part of al-Fātiḥah, or of every sūrah. Imām Abū Ḥanīfah's position was that it is not an integral part of any sūrah except an-Naml; it is an independent verse, revealed to be placed at the beginning of each sūrah in order to separate and distinguish one sūrah from another. That is a functional reading, and it accounts for the layout of the Qurʾān itself. The phrase is a divider as much as it is an opening. **What the whole sūrah is called.** Ibn Kathīr opens with a report in at-Tirmidhī, graded ṣaḥīḥ, from Abū Hurayrah: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that *al-Ḥamdu lillāhi Rabbil-ʿālamīn* is *Umm al-Qurʾān*, the Mother of the Qurʾān, and *Umm al-Kitāb*, and *as-Sabʿ al-Mathānī*, the seven oft-repeated verses, and the Glorious Qurʾān. Al-Bukhārī, at the start of his Book of Tafsīr, explains the first of those titles: it is called *Umm al-Kitāb* because the Qurʾān begins with it and because the prayer begins with its recitation. Others said it is so called because it contains the meanings of the entire Qurʾān. Imām Aḥmad records Abū Saʿīd ibn al-Muʿallā: *I was praying when the Prophet ﷺ called me, so I did not answer him until I had finished the prayer.* Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ told him he would teach him the greatest sūrah in the Qurʾān — and it was this one. Al-Bukhārī, Abū Dāwūd, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah all carry the report. Ibn Kathīr also records that the sūrah was revealed in Makkah, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and Abū al-ʿĀliyah stated. **Why it lands first.** Tazkīrul Qurʾān puts the practical meaning in a single sentence: to begin any undertaking in His Name is to acknowledge that you are God's servant, and it brings with it a divine assurance of success. The phrase is not decoration, then. It settles who is actually doing the work — and everything the rest of the sūrah says depends on that having been settled first.

2.text: *All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds.* The Arabic opens with a definite noun and a preposition: *al-ḥamdu lillāh*. Not *I praise Allah*, and not *let Allah be praised*. The sentence states that praise belongs to Allah as a fact, whether or not anyone is currently offering it. That grammatical shape does real work, and Ibn Kathīr spends most of his entry on it. Ibn Jarīr explains that *al-Ḥamdu lillāh* means all thanks are due purely to Allah alone — not to any of the objects worshipped instead of Him, and not to any of His creation. Then he adds a second layer: it is a praise that Allah praised Himself with, indicating to His servants that they too should praise Him, as if Allah had said, *Say: All thanks and praise is due to Allah.* So one clause does two things at once. It reports something true about reality, and it quietly instructs. That is why the translation renders it as a plain statement rather than a command — the instruction is carried inside the grammar, not stated over the top of it. **Why praise and not merely thanks.** Ibn Jarir is reported as saying that *al-ḥamd* entails praising Allah by mentioning His most beautiful Names and most honourable Attributes. The word is wider than gratitude. You thank someone for a specific favour; you praise them for what they are. The verse uses the wider term, and then grounds it in the wider claim: He is *Lord of all worlds*. **What the Lord of all worlds means.** The word *rabb* carries more than the English *Lord* suggests. Ibn Kathīr gives its linguistic range: master, or the one who has the authority to lead — and he notes that all these meanings are correct when applied to Allah. It is even reported that *ar-Rabb* is Allah's Greatest Name. Then *al-ʿālamīn*, the worlds. Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayd held that *ʿālam* includes everything that has a mind — the jinn, mankind, the angels and the devils. Tanwīr al-Miqbās, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbās, offers three readings in sequence: Lord of everything that has a spirit and walks upon the earth, and of the dwellers of heaven; or Master of the jinn and human beings; or the Creator of all created beings, their Provider, and the One who changes them from one state into another. Ibn ʿAbbās also explains why the praise is His in the first place. Laudation belongs to Allah because He is kind towards His created beings; because of His excessive blessings upon the servants He has guided to believe in Him; and because laudation, absolute unity and godhood all belong to Him — a God who has neither progeny, nor partner, nor helper, nor assistant. That last phrase is doing quiet work. It excludes, in advance, the three claims that the Qurʾān will spend the rest of the Book answering: that God has a son, that He has a partner, and that He needs an intermediary. **What Allah says when you recite it.** Sahīh Muslim records from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said: *Allah has said, "The prayer is divided equally between Me and My servant, and My servant shall be given what he prays for."* When the servant says *al-ḥamdu lillāhi Rabbil-ʿālamīn*, Allah says, *My servant has paid his homage to Me.* Maʿārif builds the structure of the whole sūrah out of this report. Of its seven verses, the first three are praise of Allah, the last three are a prayer from man, and the verse in the middle — *You alone we worship* — carries both. Allah has, in His mercy, taught human beings what to ask for, and then promised to answer. That is the shape to keep in view. Verses two to four describe; verse five turns; verses six and seven ask. **The weight the word carries on its own.** Ibn Kathīr gathers several reports around *al-ḥamd* itself. Imām Aḥmad records that al-Aswad ibn Sarīʿ said: *O Messenger of Allah, should I recite to you words of praise for my Lord that I have collected?* He said, *Verily, your Lord loves al-ḥamd.* An-Nasāʾī carries it too. At-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah record from Jābir ibn ʿAbdullah that the Prophet ﷺ said: *The best remembrance is Lā ilāha illallāh, and the best supplication is al-ḥamdu lillāh.* At-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan gharīb. Ibn Mājah records from Anas ibn Mālik: *No servant is blessed by Allah and says al-ḥamdu lillāh, except that what he was given is better than what he acquired himself.* And from Ibn ʿUmar, the Prophet ﷺ reporting a servant who said: *O my Lord, to You belongs the praise as befits the Majesty of Your Face and the Greatness of Your Dominion.* Al-Mukhtaṣar compresses all of it: all praise belongs to Allah with respect to His essence, His attributes and His actions, because He is the Creator of everything, everything belongs to Him, and He is the disposer of their affairs. Three grounds, then, and the verse names only the third. He is praised for what He is, for how He is described, and for what He has done — and *Lord of all worlds* is the one of those that anyone can verify by looking up.

3.text: *The Most Compassionate, Most Merciful.* Four words in English, two in Arabic, and both of them already appeared one verse ago inside the opening phrase. Why repeat them here, as a verse in their own right? Because the first three verses are doing different jobs, and this one is the hinge between them. The sūrah has just said that all praise belongs to Allah as *Lord of all worlds* — a title of authority. Authority, unqualified, is frightening. The repetition of the two names of mercy immediately after it tells you what kind of Lord you are dealing with before you are asked to stand in front of Him. Maʿārif-ul-Qurʾān makes the point explicitly. Both *Raḥmān* and *Raḥīm* are intensive forms in Arabic, and they connote the superabundance and the perfection of divine mercy respectively. And the reason this particular attribute is mentioned here, Maʿārif suggests, is to remind the reader of something easily missed: it is not through any external compulsion, nor any inner need, nor any necessity of any kind that Allah has taken on the nurturing of His entire creation. He does it in response to the demand of His own quality of mercy. If this universe did not exist, He would suffer no loss. If it does exist, it is no burden to Him. That is the difference the two names mark. A master sustains what he needs. This Lord sustains what He does not need, which is why the sustaining is mercy rather than management. **What mercy means here.** Al-Jalālayn gives the shortest definition in the corpus: the One who possesses *mercy*, which means to will what is good for those who deserve it. Note the shape of that. It is not sentiment. It is willing good — an act of will directed at a deserving object. Tanwīr al-Miqbās renders both words as *the Gentle*, which is a different angle on the same thing: mercy as the manner in which power is exercised rather than as a feeling behind it. **The report that keeps the two names honest.** Ibn Kathīr's entry on this verse is short, and he uses it for a single ḥadīth, recorded by Muslim: *If the believer knew what punishment Allah has, no one would hope to acquire His Paradise; and if the disbeliever knew what mercy Allah has, no one would despair of earning it.* Set beside the two names, that report explains why they are repeated rather than merely stated. Mercy that is announced once can be forgotten. Mercy that is announced twice, in the second verse of the sūrah that opens the whole Book, is there to be remembered at the moment the reader is most tempted to despair of it. **Why two words where one would do.** Al-Mukhtaṣar's note on the same pair is that both derive from *raḥmah* and that their doubling establishes the greatness and vastness of His mercy — that it surrounds everything and embraces all living beings, and that every blessing is due to it. So the repetition is not redundancy. The first occurrence, inside *In the Name of Allah*, attaches mercy to the act of beginning. The second, standing alone as a verse, attaches mercy to the Lord Himself. One says the work starts in mercy; the other says the Worker is merciful by nature.

4.text: *Master of the Day of Judgment.* Three verses in, the sūrah has established mercy twice and lordship once. Now it introduces time. The Arabic is *Māliki yawmi'd-dīn*. Maʿārif-ul-Qurʾān works through both words. *Mālik* comes from the root *m-l-k*, which signifies possessing a thing in such a manner that one has both the right and the power to dispose of it as one likes. *Dīn* here means requital. So the phrase means total mastery on the Day of Requital. But notice what Maʿārif notices next: the verse does not say mastery *over what*. The object is missing. According to al-Kashshāf, the omission is a general reference covering everything — on the Day of Requital, mastery over everything that exists will belong to Allah alone. That is a large claim carried by a small grammatical gap, and it is the same technique the sūrah used in its first verse. **Why that day and not another.** Al-Jalālayn answers directly: the specific mention of the Day of Judgment is because the mastery of no one else will appear on that Day except His. He cites the Qurʾān's own scene for it — *Whose is the Kingdom today?* and the answer, *Allah's* (40:16). Tanwīr al-Miqbās puts it as arbitration: He is the Arbitrator on the Day of Judgment, the Day of Reckoning and the settlement of disputes between created beings, the Day when people are judged according to their deeds — and there is no judge save Him. **What Ibn ʿAbbās made of it.** Ibn Kathīr's entry rests almost entirely on him. Ad-Daḥḥāk reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said: *On that Day, no one owns anything that they used to own in the world.* Then Ibn ʿAbbās himself: *Yawm ad-Dīn is the Day of Recompense for the creatures, meaning the Day of Judgment. On that Day, Allah will reckon the creation for their deeds — evil for evil, good for good — except for those whom He pardons.* Ibn Kathīr adds that several of the Companions, the Tābiʿūn and the scholars of the Salaf said the same, because the meaning is apparent and clear from the verse. **A reading difference worth knowing.** Al-Jalālayn records that the word can be read *mālik* or *malik*. Read as *mālik*, it signifies that He has possession of the entire affair on the Day of Resurrection. Read as *malik*, He is described by it permanently, in the same way that He is described as *Forgiver of sin* — which makes it valid as an adjective of a definite noun. Either reading says something the other does not: one that His ownership is total on that Day, the other that His kingship is not confined to it. **Why it lands here, between mercy and prayer.** The verse sits between the two names of mercy and the first request. Read in sequence, the argument runs: He is merciful by nature, and He is the sole Master of the Day when accounts are settled. Mercy without judgment would be sentiment; judgment without mercy would be terror. The sūrah holds both in one line, and only then does it let you ask for anything. Ad-Dīn means the reckoning, the reward or the punishment, and Ibn Kathīr closes with a ḥadīth that turns the word back on the reader: *The wise person is the one who reckons himself and works for what comes after death* — meaning he holds himself to account now, rather than waiting to be accounted for then.

5.text: *You ˹alone˺ we worship and You ˹alone˺ we ask for help.* Read the bracketed word carefully, because the translation is telling you something the English word order cannot. The Arabic is *Iyyāka naʿbudu wa iyyāka nastaʿīn* — *You we worship, and You we ask for help.* The object comes before the verb, twice. In Arabic, fronting the object like that restricts the action to it. It is not *we worship You* among other things we worship; it is *You — and no other — we worship*. The translation marks this with *˹alone˺* in brackets, which is the honest way to show that the emphasis is in the original and not added. Ibn Kathīr states the effect plainly: *You* means we worship You alone and none else, and we rely on You alone and none else. **What worship actually means.** Ibn Kathīr opens with the linguistics, and they are surprising. *ʿIbādah* comes from a root meaning *subdued* — a paved road is called *muʿabbadah*, beaten flat and brought under use. Worship, in its root sense, is not primarily a feeling of reverence. It is being brought under, made serviceable, having your own direction replaced by another's. That is why the verse pairs it with seeking help. If worship is being brought under someone's direction, the next question is inevitable: whose power are you relying on to stay there? **Why the order matters.** Ibn Kathīr draws out the method: this is the best way of seeking help — first praising the One from whom help is sought, then asking. The sūrah has spent four verses establishing who Allah is before it lets a single request through. Verse five is the pivot, and Ibn Kathīr notes that it is the point at which the recitation turns from description to address. Notice too the change of person. Verses two to four speak *about* Allah in the third person — *All praise is for Allah*, *Master of the Day of Judgment*. Verse five speaks *to* Him. The one who has understood who Allah is can no longer talk about Him in the abstract. Maʿārif makes this the structural centre of the whole sūrah. Of its seven verses, the first three are praise, the last three are a prayer, and this verse between the two sets has both features at once — an aspect of praise and an aspect of prayer. It is the hinge. **What the two halves divide.** Al-Jalālayn separates them cleanly: we reserve worship for You alone, by way of acknowledging Your Oneness, *tawḥīd*; and we ask for Your assistance in worship and in other things. That second half is broader than it first appears. Help is sought not only for religious acts but *in other things* — which means the verse covers every situation where a person needs support, not only the ones that happen in prayer. Tanwīr al-Miqbās renders the first half as turning to You as the only God and obeying You, and the second as asking for help in worshipping You and obtaining from You the confidence to obey You. The help requested is help *to keep worshipping*, which makes the verse partly self-referential: it asks for the ability to do what it is itself doing. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the exclusion that the fronted grammar implies: we worship and obey none except You, we associate no one with You, and from You alone do we ask for help in all our affairs. All goodness is in Your hand, and there is no helper except You. **Why this verse is the middle of the sūrah.** Ibn Kathīr records the report from Sahīh Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, in which Allah says: *I divided the prayer into two halves between Myself and My servant — one half is for Me, one half for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked.* When the servant reaches *iyyāka naʿbudu wa iyyāka nastaʿīn*, Allah says: *This is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked.* Worship is His half. The help is yours. The verse is the exact point where the two halves meet, which is why it sits in the middle rather than at either end. Ibn ʿAbbās, via ad-Daḥḥāk, gives the interior of the first half: *It is You whom we single out, Whom we fear and Whom we hope in, You alone, our Lord, and none else.* Fear and hope, held together, directed at one Object. That is what the sūrah means by worship.

6.text: *Guide us along the Straight Path.* Four verses of description and address have passed. This is the first thing the sūrah actually asks for — and it asks for guidance, not for anything you can hold. The request comes after the praise, and Ibn Kathīr is explicit that the sequence is the method: this is the best way of seeking help, by first praising the one from whom help is sought. You do not begin with the need. You begin with who can meet it. **What the word for guidance means.** Ibn Kathīr works through the root. *Ihdinā* means guide, direct, lead, and grant us the correct guidance — and he shows the range by citing the Qurʾān against itself. *And shown him the two ways* (90:10) means We explained to him the paths of good and evil. *He chose him and guided him to a straight path* (16:121). *And lead them on to the way of flaming Fire* (37:23) — the same verb, used for leading into Hell. *And verily, you are indeed guiding mankind to the straight path* (42:52). *All praise and thanks be to Allah, Who has guided us to this* (7:43), meaning He guided us, directed us and qualified us for that end, Paradise. The verb covers everything from merely being shown a road to being made fit to walk it. That range matters, because the request in this verse needs the whole of it. Maʿārif brings in the best lexical treatment available: Imām Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, in his *Mufradāt al-Qurʾān*, defines *hidāyah* as leading someone towards his destination, gently and kindly. The last two words carry the most weight. Guidance in this sense is not being told where to go and left to manage. It is being conducted to the destination, kindly, by the one who knows the way. **What the Straight Path is.** Imām Abū Jaʿfar aṭ-Ṭabarī, quoted by Ibn Kathīr, records the consensus: the ummah agreed that *aṣ-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm* is, in the language of the Arabs, the clear path without branches. Maʿārif develops the same image and gives it its theological edge. The straight path is the way of faith that equally avoids the two extremes of excess and deficiency. Whoever follows it goes neither beyond the limits nor falls short of them, in matters of doctrine and of practice both. That is a demanding definition, because it makes error possible in two directions. The straight path is not simply the opposite of irreligion; it is the narrow line between overreach and negligence, and you can leave it by being too severe as easily as by being too lax. **The parable that explains it.** Imām Aḥmad records in his Musnad, from an-Nawwās ibn Samʿān, that the Prophet ﷺ said: *Allah has set an example: a straight path, with two walls on either side of it, and in the walls open doors covered with hanging curtains. At the gate of the path stands a caller saying, "O people, enter the path all together and do not deviate," and above the path there is another caller. If a person tries to open any of those doors, he says, "Woe to you, do not open it, for if you open it you will enter it." The path is Islam; the two walls are the limits set by Allah; the open doors are what Allah has prohibited; the caller at the head of the path is the Book of Allah; and the caller above the path is the admonisher of Allah in the heart of every Muslim.* Two callers, then — one outside you in the text, one inside you in the conscience — and the doors are not locked. They are curtained. Nothing stops you; you simply have to lift the covering, which is exactly how a prohibited thing usually presents itself. **The objection, and why it fails.** Both Ibn Kathīr and Maʿārif raise the same question, because it is the first one any careful reader asks. Why does a believer pray for guidance in every single prayer, when he is already guided? Maʿārif sharpens it further: the request is addressed equally to all people, and to the saints and prophets who have not only received guidance but are themselves a source of guidance for others. Why should they keep praying for something they already possess? Ibn Kathīr's answer is short and decisive: if it were not a fact that the believer needs to keep asking for guidance day and night, Allah would not have directed him to ask for it. Maʿārif's answer goes deeper and rests on Rāghib's definition. Because *hidāyah* means being conducted to a destination gently, it is not a possession you acquire once. It is a relationship you remain inside. You can be guided and still need guiding, in the way that a person walking a road with a guide still needs the guide at every step. **What is being asked for, specifically.** Tanwīr al-Miqbās offers three readings: guide us to the established Religion with which You are pleased, that is Islam; or make us firm in holding fast to it; or — the straight path refers to Allah's Book, and guidance to it means guidance to what it prescribes as lawful and unlawful. Al-Mukhtaṣar combines two of them: show us and make easy for us the right way, the path of submission to You which has no crookedness, and make us firm upon it. Al-Jalālayn is briefest: *guide us to the straight path*, that is, show us the way to it. Between them the request has four parts — to be shown the way, to be made able to walk it, to be kept on it, and to be brought to its end. The single Arabic verb carries all four, which is why the verse is short and the tafsīr on it is not.

7.text: *The path of those You have blessed—not those You are displeased with, or those who are astray.* The previous verse asked for the straight path in the abstract. This one identifies it, and it does so in the way a person actually learns a road: not from a definition, but from who has already walked it and who has not. The verse has three parts, and the structure is not symmetrical. One group is named positively. Two are named by what went wrong. **Who has been blessed.** Maʿārif answers from the Qurʾān itself rather than from opinion, citing 4:69: *Those whom Allah has blessed — namely, the prophets, the ṣiddīqūn, the shuhadāʾ, and the righteous.* Four categories, in descending rank. The prophets are the greatest. The *ṣiddīqūn*, the constantly truthful, are those who acquire spiritual perfection and so attain the highest rank among the followers of a prophet — in common speech, the people of Allah, or saints. The *shuhadāʾ* are those who sacrifice even their lives for their faith, or who bear witness to the truth, since the word admits both meanings. And the *ṣāliḥūn* are those who follow the Sharīʿah completely, in obligation and in recommendation alike. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the same four and adds a line worth pausing on: *what good companions these people make.* The verse is not only identifying a route; it is telling you who you will be walking with, which is a different kind of reassurance. **The two groups excluded, and the difference between them.** This is where the verse does its sharpest work, because the two negatives are not the same failure. Al-Mukhtaṣar distinguishes them precisely. Those who earned anger are those *who knew the truth and did not follow it* — as was the case with the Israelites. Those who went astray are those who *lost their way and were not guided because they were neglectful in seeking the truth* — as was the case with the Christians. Knowledge without action, on one side. Effort without knowledge, on the other. Both miss the straight path, and neither is the opposite of the other — they are opposite errors, which is exactly what Maʿārif's definition of the straight path as the avoidance of two extremes predicts. Ibn Kathīr carries the report that fixes the identification. Imām Aḥmad records from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim — whose aunt was taken by the Prophet's horsemen and then freed, after which ʿAdī himself embraced Islam — that the Prophet ﷺ said: *Those who have earned the anger are the Jews, and those who are led astray are the Christians.* At-Tirmidhī collected it too and called it ḥasan gharīb. Tanwīr al-Miqbās, from Ibn ʿAbbās, reads the first group more narrowly in time: the religion of those You blessed, the followers of Moses before the blessings of Allah deserted them — when He shaded them with a white cloud and sent down manna and quails in the wilderness. The point is that the exclusion is of a condition, not of a people as such; the same community is praised at one moment in its history and excluded at another. **A grammatical detail that carries the meaning.** Al-Jalālayn notes the construction. *The path of those whom You have favoured* is followed by a substitution — the phrase *not the path of those against whom there is wrath* replaces it grammatically. And the subtle meaning implied by that substitution, he writes, is that the guided ones are neither the Jews nor the Christians. The exclusion is built into the syntax, not merely stated in the words. **What the reader says at the end.** *Amin.* It is not part of the verse, but Ibn Kathīr treats it here because it belongs here. *Amin* means *O Allah, accept our invocation.* The evidence that saying it is recommended is what Imāms Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd and at-Tirmidhī recorded from Wāʾil ibn Ḥujr: *I heard the Messenger of Allah recite "not the way of those who earned Your anger, nor of those who went astray," and he said "Amin," extending it with his voice.* Abū Dāwūd's narration adds, *raising his voice with it.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās offers two glosses on the word: let it be so; or, *O our Lord, do with us as we have requested You.* **Why the sūrah ends here.** Tazkīrul Qurʾān describes this opening chapter as a miniature portrayal of Islamic belief, and reading the seven verses in order shows why. A person looks at the world and cannot miss God's power and mercy in evidence everywhere. Everything has been adapted to human need so precisely that the cosmic machine cannot be in vain. Therefore there must come a day when the grateful and the ungrateful are rewarded for how they lived. And having seen that, the person turns and says: Lord, You are the Master of the Day of Judgment; I have submitted to You and humbly seek Your help; show me the path that is, to You, the true path; keep me with those You have chosen; and keep me from the path of those who went astray, and from the path of those who earned Your wrath through obstinacy. That sequence — observation, recognition, submission, request — is the whole argument of the Qurʾān in seven verses. The rest of the Book is the working out.
